title: After 3 weeks and 3,170 commits, I'm ready to share my 5v5 RTS game that's a mixture of Age of Empires, Starcraft, Warcraft 3 and League of Legends.
author: DreamPlayPianos
selftext:
I started this project October 18 last month. 3 weeks/3k+ commits later I'm ready to share this project with the world (first demo/playtest version). It's completely free to play, no login required, no download at all. A great game to play after you just gave your AI a 50 item PRD and you know it's gonna take them a while to finish.

[https://ultimate.army](https://ultimate.army)

A bit of background: I'm a musician and previously a financial analyst. I grew up playing RTS games like Starcraft, Age of Empires, and Warcraft 3, and my favorite thing about those games were the epic mid to late game battles that seemed to last forever with both sides constantly supplying units into the battlefield. 

So for this ultimate army game, I had one goal: to maximize that feeling as much as possible while minimizing cognitive load elsewhere. I created 3 races, humans orcs and elves. Eventually I want to have 12, but the game has to work with 3 before it can expand.

And of course, I was also a League addict back in the day, so I also threw in heroes and spells and items. 

How the game goes: You are on a side with 4 other allies, vs 5 enemies. Similar to a MOBA. there are 5 lanes that go to the opposing player's side. In the middle of the map are 5 gold flags that you have to captures, as well as 8 energy crystals (4 on each side of the river). 

Unlike regular MOBAs, you choose the army composition that goes into battle. Pressing 1 buys an Infantry block, 2 creates a Ranged block, 3 creates a Siege block. Each block produces 1 unit per X seconds based on a timer based on how powerful the unit is (for example an infantry block is 1 unit per second, a siege is 1 unit per 2.5 seconds). 

You can also buy upgrades for your units. Every purchase you make increases the price of the next purchase, so you have to be strategic about whether you make upgrades or produce soldiers, and which soldiers or upgrades you take. Since your opponent is making the same decisions in real time, the person with the better strategy will eventually win.

The result is a chaotic, constantly evolving battlefield where both sides constantly have units marching in and fighting to the death, and the heros in this game are different than traditional MOBAs - here they are basically supporting cast and the armies themselves are the main characters. 

But what's really interesting to me, is the strategies that goes into this game. You can go for an early-game rush and do hero summons directly to your hero, but you give up later game economy. You can go full eco with your deck strategy, but you might be uncompetitive for the flags. You can go hardcore into archers, but you'll get countered by someone who maximizes AOE spells like meteor storm that wipes out platoons of archers in seconds. 

Here's what I used to make it:

\- Claude Code (Opus 5.5 extra high) and Codex for image gen, Meshy for 3d

\- ECS design principles (so that we can have over 5k units onscreen at the same time without lagging the browser). The game gets 40+ fps with 3000 units on the map. 

\- No game engine, just plain JavaScript and Three.js with no build step, so it runs in the browser

\- 2D art drawn by Codex, 3D models from Meshy

\- Music, sound effects and the trailer's narration from ElevenLabs

\- Tons of small decisions on the counters (every unit has one) and the balance, and to be honest the balance is the part I still fiddle with the most (probably 50% of my work is just balancing the 3 races and their units)

Edit: It's still very much a work in progress, currently in the "playtest" stage. I'm still working on the visuals, and recently introduced a "bold" style of artwork and animations. The reason why artwork and animations takes a backburner for me is because of 2 reasons:

1. I care the most about the gameplay and the balancing. I prioritize more the depth of strategy, the unit and hero mechanics, and how each race "feels". If people start playing this game and creating different strategies for it, then I'll look into upgrading the graphics more. 
2. As a web browser game, we simply can't compete with installed games for GPU usage. The game is designed to handle 5,000 units onscreen at the same time at 30 fps (3000 units for 60fps) along with animations and summoner spells. 

It's free to play right in your browser at [https://ultimate.army](https://ultimate.army/), no download and no login required. 

Feedback would be greatly appreciated! 

Edit: I'm looking for feedback specifically in 3 areas:

1) Is the game fun to play? Is it clear what's going on, and do you get a good feel for the game within the first match, or is it completely chaotic and makes no sense?

2) Is the layout confusing? Given there are heroes, spells, cards, upgrades, summons, drafts, and items to deal with, I wonder if everything is explained clearly.

3) Does it lag when army sizes increase? I'm 99% confident it won't lag for full-game battles for most users, but people on their phones or on older computers might experience lower FPS numbers.

comments.author: teapot_RGB_color
comments.body:
Okay, I try it.. not for long.

  
I get a strong feeling like you kept adding features during development here and never stopped to ask, "hey is this fun", but brute forced your way forward instead. Is this correct.

I get the blizzard inspiration here, but you should really go back and open up warcraft 3 again, look at  the details, how the camera moves when you wasd your way around the map, the tiny reactions to the heros when you select them. The animations of sprites when you select things. WC3, is very old at this point, but it is also a very good benchmark how to approach getting games to "Feel" right and feel good.

replies.author: DreamPlayPianos
replies.body: That's really great advice. There's actually a lot of features that I already took out, but I do realize it's a lot. If there was one thing you would take out, what would it be?

comments.author: RenTroutGaming
comments.body:
Are you sure you played those games you reference? When during those games do you just funnel an endless wave of units into a small choke? I'm most familiar with SC and AoE, and in neither of those are you just throwing massive units into the grinder. 

\> But what's really interesting to me, is the strategies that goes into this game. You can go for an early-game rush and do hero summons directly to your hero, but you give up later game economy. You can go full eco with your deck strategy, but you might be uncompetitive for the flags. You can go hardcore into archers, but you'll get countered by someone who maximizes AOE spells like meteor storm that wipes out platoons of archers in seconds. 

I guess except for that there are 1,000 flash games that do exactly this, or you can play one of the billion clones of Clash of Clans on the iOS/Android stores. This really simple rock paper scissors isn't that interesting because its been done hundreds of times before Claude copied it.

\>The result is a chaotic, constantly evolving battlefield where both sides constantly have units marching in and fighting to the death,

What is constantly evolving here? The paths from early to mid to late game are very straightforward. There doesn't appear to be infrastructure supporting either army (like in SC or AoE, and to a lesser extend W3). 

\>Since your opponent is making the same decisions in real time, the person with the better strategy will eventually win

Ehhhh... maybe. The problem with these "timer" or "mana" based games is that it really reduces unit production to a pretty simple yes/no choice. All of the games you've previously listed (SC, AoE, W3) have varying degrees of information that informs decision making. Games like this come down to more "Oh, I see a bunch of archers running from his castle, better prep my anti-archer spell!" Think about how MOBAs (and SC, AoE, W3) have both a macro and micro layer and how important that micro layer is, these vibe coded games that run off java in a browser can never really recreate that. So you have to figure out what takes that place, and hitting 1,2, or 3 on your keyboard in rhythm with your opponent isn't it.

replies.author: DreamPlayPianos
replies.body:
>What is constantly evolving here? The paths from early to mid to late game are very straightforward. There doesn't appear to be infrastructure supporting either army (like in SC or AoE, and to a lesser extend W3).

Well, it's not really meant to be a full RTS. It's really just meant to be an autobattler where you select different army comps. I guess labeling it RTS is kind of a mislabel.

>Games like this come down to more "Oh, I see a bunch of archers running from his castle, better prep my anti-archer spell!"

Yes, the point is each unit has a counter, but that counter also has its own counter. If you spend resources upgrading your own anti-archer spell, you'll eventually get overrun by cavalry. Every choice you make has an opportunity cost.

Really appreciate your feedback though, I think you made some great points!
